You look tired. How did last week go in Miami?
It was a long week. On Monday a client called at seven in the morning about a shipment that never left the port.
We did, on Wednesday. The exporter sent the wrong document, so the terminal did not release the cargo.
And the client? Did he accept that?
Not at first. I spent Thursday on the phone with him and with two colleagues in Houston. We postponed the delivery and agreed on a new date.
So when did you finally close it?
On Friday afternoon. Three drafts, one bad document, and one signature at four o’clock. It went well, in the end.

Good morning. Before we start, here is what happened last week, in five minutes. On Monday the buyer in Rotterdam sent us the first draft, and it arrived with two clauses nobody expected. I read it on Monday night and I called the client on Tuesday morning. He was not happy. On Wednesday we sent our version back, and they accepted most of it. Then the ship was late, and everything stopped for two days. Nobody called us, and nobody explained why. On Friday the other side finally answered, we agreed on a new date, and the client signed at four o'clock. So: one week, three drafts, one delay, and one signature. I want you to remember that week, because next month one of you runs a matter like it on your own.

In nineteen seventy-two the Soviet Union bought almost a quarter of the American wheat crop, and almost nobody in Washington noticed. The Soviet buyers went to five different trading houses in New York in the same month. Each house thought it sold a normal cargo, because nobody talked to anybody else. When the government finally counted the ships, the grain was already at sea. The price of bread went up in every American supermarket that year, and the newspapers called it the great grain robbery. Nothing illegal happened. Five contracts, five signatures, and five lawyers who did their job properly. So the lesson is not really about wheat. It is about information. Every one of those contracts was correct, and the deal was still a disaster, because nobody asked the same question at the same time.
